extraction_notes.note: The float holding Figures 2 and 3 sits inside the proof of Lemma 1, and its caption's (a)/(b) panel markers are detected as author labels that must start steps; the float became an 'other' step with the two caption panels as children, and the caption's refs to Lemmas 1 and 2 are mention edges.

The prose argument for the arbitrary-radii corollary starts with a motivating sentence ('We may also generalize...') and ends at 'we obtain the following corollary.'; the whole paragraph was taken as its proof.
Lemma environment the authors call 'a simple fact' with no proof given; kept as lemma (paper origin) with semi_formal rigor rather than external standard.
The Fox-Pach theorem is stated twice in prose (Introduction and Section 4.1) with no environment or number; the Introduction copy was kept and the Section 4.1 restatement got no node.

The inline 'We now show that ... m' ...' opener ends a paragraph; its argument spans the next several paragraphs, so the claim step was nested over them up to 'That is, ...' rather than stopping at the paragraph break.

Experimental setup details (hardware, parameter sweeps, the brute-force arrangement and FCS implementation, the O(n^3) optimal-separator implementation) and figure-only results were not extracted; only the two stated empirical findings became numerical remarks.

nodes.name: alpha-separator
nodes.statement: Given an undirected graph $G=(V,E)$ with $V$ as its vertex set and $E$ as its edge set, and a non-negative real number $\alpha \in [1/2,1]$, we say that a subset $S\subseteq V$ is an \emph{$\alpha$-separator} if the vertex set of $G \setminus S$ can be partitioned into two sets $A$ and $B$, each of size at most $\alpha |V|$ such that there is no edge between $A$ and $B$.
differentia: the vertex set of $G \setminus S$ can be partitioned into two sets $A$ and $B$, each of size at most $\alpha |V|$ such that there is no edge between $A$ and $B$
nodes.statement_short: $S$ is an $\alpha$-separator if removing it leaves two parts of size at most $\alpha|V|$ with no edge between them.

nodes.name: Lipton--Tarjan planar separator theorem
nodes.statement: For example, the well-known Lipton--Tarjan planar separator theorem~\cite{doi:10.1137/0136016} states that for any $n$-vertex planar graph, there exists a $2/3$-separator of size $O(\sqrt{n})$.
assumptions: for any $n$-vertex planar graph
conclusions: there exists a $2/3$-separator of size $O(\sqrt{n})$

nodes.name: Miller--Teng--Thurston--Vavasis sphere separator theorem
nodes.statement: They considered intersection graphs of $n$ balls in $\mathbb{R}^d$ and proved that if every point in $d$-dimensional space is covered by at most $k$ of the given balls, then there exists a $(d+1)/(d+2)$-separator of size $O(k^{1/d}n^{1-1/d})$ (and such a separator can be found in deterministic linear time~\cite{DBLP:journals/fuin/EppsteinMT95}). More interestingly, the separator itself and the two sets it creates have very nice properties; they show that there exists a $(d{-}1)$-dimensional sphere that intersects at most $O(k^{1/d}n^{1-1/d})$ balls and contains at most $(d+1)n/(d+2)$ balls in its interior and at most $(d+1)n/(d+2)$ balls in its exterior.
nodes.origin_citation: Miller, Teng, Thurston & Vavasis 1997; Smith & Wormald 1998
assumptions: intersection graphs of $n$ balls in $\mathbb{R}^d$
every point in $d$-dimensional space is covered by at most $k$ of the given balls
conclusions: there exists a $(d+1)/(d+2)$-separator of size $O(k^{1/d}n^{1-1/d})$

there exists a $(d{-}1)$-dimensional sphere that intersects at most $O(k^{1/d}n^{1-1/d})$ balls and contains at most $(d+1)n/(d+2)$ balls in its interior and at most $(d+1)n/(d+2)$ balls in its exterior
nodes.statement_short: Intersection graphs of $k$-ply balls in $\mathbb{R}^d$ have a sphere separator of size $O(k^{1/d}n^{1-1/d})$ with balance $(d+1)/(d+2)$.

nodes.name: Ply-dependence of the sphere separator bound
nodes.statement: The bound on the separator size does not hold up well when $k$ is large, even for $d=2$: if $\sqrt{n}$ disks overlap at a single point and the other disks form a path we have $k=\sqrt{n}$ and $m=\Theta(n)$, where $m$ is the number of edges in the intersection graph. Hence, the separator has size $O(\sqrt{kn})=O(m^{3/4})$.
nodes.statement_short: With $\sqrt{n}$ disks through one point plus a path, $k=\sqrt{n}$, $m=\Theta(n)$ and the sphere separator has size $O(m^{3/4})$.

nodes.name: Fox--Pach separator theorem
nodes.statement: Fox and Pach~\cite{Fox20081070} gave another separator result that follows the same spirit: the intersection graph of a set of Jordan curves in the plane has a $2/3$-separator of size $O(\sqrt{m})$ if every pair of curves intersects at a constant number of points.
assumptions: every pair of curves intersects at a constant number of points
conclusions: the intersection graph of a set of Jordan curves in the plane has a $2/3$-separator of size $O(\sqrt{m})$

nodes.name: Alon--Katchalski--Pulleyblank line theorem for disjoint unit disks
nodes.statement: Alon~\textit{et al.}~\cite{DBLP:journals/dcg/AlonKP89} proved that for a given set $\cal{D}$ of $n$ pairwise disjoint unit disks,\footnote{The result extends to pairwise disjoint fat objects that are convex and of similar area (see Theorem 4.1 of~\cite{DBLP:journals/dcg/AlonKP89}). For the sake of conciseness we only talk about unit disks.} there exists a slope $a$ such that every line with slope $a$ intersects $O(\sqrt{n \log n})$ unit disks of $\cal{D}$.
assumptions: a given set $\cal{D}$ of $n$ pairwise disjoint unit disks
conclusions: there exists a slope $a$ such that every line with slope $a$ intersects $O(\sqrt{n \log n})$ unit disks of $\cal{D}$

nodes.name: Hoffmann et al. balanced line separator for disjoint unit disks
nodes.statement: A deterministic $O(n)$-time algorithm was afterwards given by Hoffmann~\textit{et al.}~\cite{DBLP:conf/esa/HoffmannKM14}, who also showed how to find a line $\ell$ that intersects at most $O(\sqrt{n/(1-2\alpha)})$ unit disks and each halfplane contains at most $(1-\alpha)n$ disks (for any $0 < \alpha < 1/2$).
assumptions: for any $0 < \alpha < 1/2$
conclusions: find a line $\ell$ that intersects at most $O(\sqrt{n/(1-2\alpha)})$ unit disks and each halfplane contains at most $(1-\alpha)n$ disks
nodes.statement_short: Deterministic linear-time line separators of disjoint unit disks crossing $O(\sqrt{n/(1-2\alpha)})$ disks with balance $1-\alpha$.

nodes.name: Loffler--Mulzer axis-parallel separator
nodes.statement: L\"offler and Mulzer \cite{DBLP:journals/jocg/LofflerM14} proved that there exists an axis-parallel line $\ell$ such that $\ell$ intersects $O(\sqrt{n})$ disks, and each halfplane contains at most $9n/10$ unit disks, and such line can be found in $O(n)$ time.
conclusions: there exists an axis-parallel line $\ell$ such that $\ell$ intersects $O(\sqrt{n})$ disks, and each halfplane contains at most $9n/10$ unit disks
such line can be found in $O(n)$ time

nodes.name: Fu--Wang grid line separator
nodes.statement: Fu and Wang \cite{DBLP:journals/siamcomp/FuW07} studied the case where a unit disk graph is a $\sqrt{n}\times\sqrt{n}$ grid generated from a regular grid, and proved that there exists a line $2/3$-separator of size at most $1.129\sqrt{n}$.
assumptions: a unit disk graph is a $\sqrt{n}\times\sqrt{n}$ grid generated from a regular grid
conclusions: there exists a line $2/3$-separator of size at most $1.129\sqrt{n}$

nodes.name: Fu--Oprisan--Xu improved grid line separator
nodes.statement: The bound of $1.129\sqrt{n}$ was afterwards improved by Fu~\textit{et al.}~\cite{DBLP:journals/ijcga/FuOX08} to $1.02074\sqrt{n}$.
conclusions: The bound of $1.129\sqrt{n}$ was afterwards improved by Fu~\textit{et al.}~\cite{DBLP:journals/ijcga/FuOX08} to $1.02074\sqrt{n}$.

nodes.name: Polynomial-time minimum 2/3-separator of unit disk graphs
nodes.statement: We note that it is not known whether a minimum-size $2/3$-separator of a unit disk graph can be computed in polynomial time, although the problem is known to be NP-hard for graphs of maximum degree three \cite{DBLP:journals/ipl/BuiJ92}, $3$-regular graphs \cite{DBLP:journals/computing/MullerW91}, and planar graphs \cite{DBLP:journals/jgaa/Fukuyama06}.
nodes.statement_short: Unknown whether a minimum-size $2/3$-separator of a unit disk graph is computable in polynomial time (NP-hard for related classes).

nodes.name: unit disk
nodes.statement: In this paper, all disks are assumed to be closed (i.e., the boundaries are part of the disks), and a \emph{unit disk} has radius one (thus diameter two).

nodes.name: Centerpoint theorem
nodes.statement: For a set $S$ of $n$ points in $\mathbb{R}^2$, there always exists a point $p \in \mathbb{R}^2$ such that every halfplane containing $p$ contains at least $n/3$ points from $S$.
assumptions: a set $S$ of $n$ points in $\mathbb{R}^2$
conclusions: there always exists a point $p \in \mathbb{R}^2$ such that every halfplane containing $p$ contains at least $n/3$ points from $S$

nodes.name: centerpoint
nodes.statement: Such a point $p$ is called a \emph{centerpoint} of $S$, and can be found in $O(n)$ time \cite{DBLP:journals/dcg/JadhavM94}.
differentia: every halfplane containing $p$ contains at least $n/3$ points from $S$

nodes.name: Line through a centerpoint is 2/3-balanced
nodes.statement: Let $\ell$ be a line through a centerpoint of $S$. Then, each of the two closed halfplanes bounded by~$\ell$ contains at least $n/3$ points of $S$, which in turn means that each of the two open halfplanes bounded by $\ell$ contains at most $2n/3$ points of $S$ each.
assumptions: Let $\ell$ be a line through a centerpoint of $S$.
conclusions: each of the two closed halfplanes bounded by~$\ell$ contains at least $n/3$ points of $S$
each of the two open halfplanes bounded by $\ell$ contains at most $2n/3$ points of $S$ each

nodes.name: halfplane contains a point
nodes.statement: Here, a halfplane $H$ (closed or open) \emph{contains} a point $p$ if $p \in H$.

nodes.name: halfplane contains a disk
nodes.statement: We also say a halfplane~$H$ \emph{contains} a disk $D$ if $D \subseteq H$.

nodes.name: Random line through a point, disjoint unit disks
nodes.statement: Let $\cal{D}$ be a set of $n$ pairwise disjoint unit disks in the plane and let~$p$ be any point in the plane. Then the expected number of disks intersected by a random line through $p$ is $O(\sqrt{n})$.
assumptions: Let $\cal{D}$ be a set of $n$ pairwise disjoint unit disks in the plane
let~$p$ be any point in the plane
conclusions: the expected number of disks intersected by a random line through $p$ is $O(\sqrt{n})$

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma (disjoint unit disks)
nodes.statement: Let $C_i$ be the circle of radius $2i$ centered at $p$, for $i=0,1,\ldots$. Then each disk in ${\cal D}$ is intersected by at most two of these circles---if a disk is intersected by two circles the intersection takes place on the boundary of the disk. Let ${\cal D}_i \subseteq {\cal D}$ be the set of disks that have non-empty intersection with $C_i$, for $i=0,1,\ldots$. See \figurename~\ref{fig:disjoint_unit}. Note that $\sum_{i} |{\cal D}_i| \leq 2n$. \begin{figure}[t] \centering \begin{minipage}{0.31\textwidth} \centering \resizebox{\textwidth}{!}{\includegraphics{disjoint_unit}} \caption{Proof of Lemma \ref{lem:disjoint_unit}. The number $i$ in each disk means that it intersects the circle of radius $2i$ centered at $p$. } \end{minipage} \hfill \begin{minipage}{0.64\textwidth} \centering \resizebox{\textwidth}{!}{\includegraphics{joint_unit}} \caption{Proof of Lemma \ref{lem:joint_unit}. (a) A grid of $\sqrt{2}\times \sqrt{2}$ squares is laid over the family of unit disks. (b) Disks associated to the same cell intersect, but disks associated to different cells of the same color do not intersect. If $j$ is the index for color yellow, then $n_j = 7$, $l_{j0}=4$, and $l_{j1}=1$ in this example.} \end{minipage} \end{figure} Given a random line $\ell$ through $p$, the number $k_i$ of disks of ${\cal D}_i$ that are intersected by $\ell$ is at most four, due to disjointness, and its expectation is $O(|{\cal D}_i|/i)$. Therefore, by the linearity of expectation, the expected number of disks of $\cal{D}$ intersected by $\ell$ is bounded by \begin{align*} \mathbb{E}\left[\sum_{i \ge 0} k_i\right] &= \mathbb{E}\left[\sum_{i\colon i\leq \sqrt{n}} k_i\right] + \mathbb{E}\left[\sum_{i\colon i > \sqrt{n}} k_i\right]\\ &\le 4\sqrt{n} + \sum_{i\colon i > \sqrt{n}} O(|{\cal D}_i|/\sqrt{n}) = O(\sqrt{n}) + O(n/\sqrt{n}) = O(\sqrt{n}). \tag*{\qed} \end{align*}
nodes.statement_short: Layer disks by concentric circles of radius $2i$ around $p$; a random line meets each layer in $O(1)$ disks with probability $O(1/i)$, and summing splits at $i=\sqrt{n}$.

nodes.name: Line 2/3-separator of disjoint unit disks
nodes.statement: Let $\cal{D}$ be a set of $n$ pairwise disjoint unit disks in the plane. Then, there exists a line $\ell$ that intersects $O(\sqrt{n})$ disks of $\cal{D}$ such that each of the two open halfplanes bounded by $\ell$ contains at most $2n/3$ disks of $\cal{D}$. Moreover, such a line can be found in $O(n)$ time with probability at least $3/4$.
assumptions: Let $\cal{D}$ be a set of $n$ pairwise disjoint unit disks in the plane.
conclusions: there exists a line $\ell$ that intersects $O(\sqrt{n})$ disks of $\cal{D}$ such that each of the two open halfplanes bounded by $\ell$ contains at most $2n/3$ disks of $\cal{D}$
such a line can be found in $O(n)$ time with probability at least $3/4$
nodes.label: cor:disjoint_unit

nodes.name: Proof of Corollary (disjoint unit disks)
nodes.statement: Let $p$ be a centerpoint of the set of centers of disks in ${\cal D}$. By Lemma~\ref{lem:disjoint_unit}, some line through $p$ must intersect at most $O(\sqrt{n})$ disks from ${\cal D}$. Since $p$ is a centerpoint, each of the two open halfplanes bounded by $\ell$ contains at most $2n/3$ centers of disks in ${\cal D}$, which means that the halfplane contains at most $2n/3$ disks from ${\cal D}$. The argument above suggests the following algorithm: first we compute a centerpoint~$p$ of the centers of a given set of disks, and then choose a line through~$p$ uniformly at random. By Lemma \ref{lem:disjoint_unit} and Markov's inequality, the probability that the random line intersects more than $c\sqrt{n}$ disks is at most $1/4$ for some constant~$c$. Thus, a desired line can be found with probability at least $3/4$. The running time is linear in the number of disks since a centerpoint can be found in linear time \cite{DBLP:journals/dcg/JadhavM94}. \qed
nodes.statement_short: Take a random line through a centerpoint of the disk centers; apply the lemma with Markov's inequality.

nodes.name: Success probability 3/4 is inessential (disjoint case)
nodes.statement: In the statement above, the fact that the probability of success is $3/4$ is not important (any positive probability would have also sufficed).

nodes.name: Random line through a point, intersecting unit disks
nodes.statement: Let $\cal{D}$ be a set of $n$ unit disks in the plane with $m$ intersecting pairs, and let $p$ be any point in the plane. Then the expected number of disks intersected by a random line through $p$ is $O(\sqrt{(m+n)\log n})$.
assumptions: Let $\cal{D}$ be a set of $n$ unit disks in the plane with $m$ intersecting pairs
let $p$ be any point in the plane
conclusions: the expected number of disks intersected by a random line through $p$ is $O(\sqrt{(m+n)\log n})$
nodes.label: lem:joint_unit

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma (intersecting unit disks)
nodes.statement: Consider a grid of $\sqrt{2} \times \sqrt{2}$ squares. Each grid cell is treated as right-open and top-open so that it is of the form of $[x,x+\sqrt{2})\times [y,y+\sqrt{2})$. Associate each disk in $\cal{D}$ with the grid cell containing its center, see \figurename~\ref{fig:joint_unit}(a). Observe that one can color the grid cells with nine colors for every $3\times 3$ block of grid cells, so that no two disks that are associated with different grid cells of the same color intersect, see \figurename~\ref{fig:joint_unit}(b). Consider one of the colors $j$, with $1 \le j \le 9$, and let ${\mathbb C}_j$ be the collection of subsets of $\cal{D}$ associated with the grid cells of this color: \[ {\mathbb C}_j = \{{\cal C} \subseteq {\cal D} \mid \text{ the center of disks in } {\cal C} \text{ lie in the same grid cell of color } j\}. \] Then, ${\mathbb C}_j$ has the following two properties: (i) each subset ${\cal C} \in {\mathbb C}_j$ in the same grid cell is a clique, i.e., any two disks in the subset intersect each other; (ii) any two disks from two different subsets in ${\mathbb C}_j$ are pairwise disjoint. Let $n_j = \sum_{{\cal C} \in {\mathbb C}_j} |{\cal C}|$ denote the number of disks in ${\cal D}$ associated to grid cells of color $j$. We divide the cliques in ${\mathbb C}_j$ into $O(\log n_j)$ buckets ${\mathbb B}_{j0},{\mathbb B}_{j1},\ldots$, where ${\mathbb B}_{ji}$ consists of all cliques of ${\mathbb C}_j$ whose size is in the range $[2^i,2^{i+1})$. Set $l_{ji} = |{\mathbb B}_{ji}|$, for $i=0,1,\ldots$. Then, the sum $x_{ji}$ of the sizes of the cliques in ${\mathbb B}_{ji}$ is in the range $l_{ji}2^i \le x_{ji} < l_{ji}2^{i+1} $. We also know that $\sum_i x_{ji} = n_j$. Let $m_{ji} = \sum_{{\cal C} \in \mathbb{B}_{ji}} |{\cal C}|(|{\cal C}|-1)/2$ denote the number of pairs of intersecting disks within ${\mathbb B}_{ji}$. Then, $l_{ji} (2^{2i-1}-2^{i-1}) \le m_{ji} < l_{ji} (2^{2i+1}-2^{i})$ and $\sum_i m_{ji} \le \sum_j \sum_i m_{ji} \leq m.$ We first compute the expected number of disks in cliques of ${\mathbb B}_{ji}$ intersected by a random line through $p$. Since the union of the disks in each clique is contained in a disk of radius 2 such that these disks of radius 2 are disjoint, a random line through $p$ intersects only $O(\sqrt{l_{ji}})$ cliques of ${\mathbb B}_{ji}$ by Lemma~\ref{lem:disjoint_unit}, and therefore only $O(\sqrt{l_{ji}}2^{i+1})$ disks of~${\cal D}$. By the definition of ${\mathbb B}_{ji}$, we have $l_{ji}2^{2i-1} \leq m_{ji} + l_{ji} 2^{i-1} \leq m_{ji} + x_{ji}/2$. Thus, a random line through $p$ intersects $O(\sqrt{m_{ji} + x_{ji}})$ disks in expectation. Then, by the linearity of expectation, we sum the numbers for all $j=1, \ldots, 9$ and $i = 0, \ldots, \log n_j$: \begin{eqnarray*} \sum_j \sum_i O(\sqrt{m_{ji} + x_{ji}}) &\leq& O\left(\sqrt{\sum_j \sum_i (m_{ji} + x_{ji})} \sqrt{\sum_j \sum_i 1}\right)\\ &\leq& O(\sqrt{(m+n)\log n}), \end{eqnarray*} where the first inequality follows from the Cauchy--Schwarz inequality. \qed
nodes.statement_short: Grid of $\sqrt2$-cells with a 9-coloring makes cliques per color; bucket cliques by size, apply the disjoint lemma per bucket and sum with Cauchy--Schwarz.

nodes.name: Proof of Theorem (line separator of unit disks)
nodes.statement: In the same way as Corollary~\ref{cor:disjoint_unit} follows from Lemma~\ref{lem:disjoint_unit}, the following theorem follows from Lemma~\ref{lem:joint_unit}.
nodes.statement_short: Same as the corollary for disjoint disks: random line through a centerpoint, using the intersecting-disks lemma.

conclusions: there exists a line $\ell$ that intersects $O(\sqrt{(m+n)\log n})$ disks of ${\cal D}$ such that each of the two open halfplanes bounded by $\ell$ contains at most $2n/3$ disks of ${\cal D}$

nodes.name: Success probability 3/4 is inessential (general case)

nodes.name: Lemma holds for radii between 1 and 2
nodes.statement: We here note that Lemma \ref{lem:joint_unit} also holds even when the radii of all disks range between $1$ and $2$.

conclusions: Lemma \ref{lem:joint_unit} also holds

conclusions: Theorem \ref{thm:joint_unit} also holds in such a case.

nodes.name: Proof sketch for radii between 1 and 2
nodes.statement: To adopt the proof of Lemma \ref{lem:joint_unit}, we change the coloring of the grid cells. Namely, we color with 36 colors for every $6\times 6$ block of grid cells, so that no two disks that are associated with different grid cells of the same color intersect. Then, the same argument works, and we obtain the lemma.
nodes.statement_short: Rerun the grid argument with a 36-coloring of $6\times 6$ blocks of cells.

nodes.name: Proof of Corollary (arbitrary radii)
nodes.statement: We may also generalize the argument when the radii of the disks are arbitrary. Let $\cal{D}$ be a set of disks of arbitrary radii. Then, we classify the disks in $\cal{D}$ by their radii. By scaling, we assume that the smallest radius of the disks is one. Let $\Delta$ be the radius of a largest disk (or, before scaling, the ratio between the smallest and the largest radius of the disks). Then, for each $i = 1,2,\dots,\lceil \log_2 \Delta \rceil$, the set ${\cal D}_i \subseteq \cal{D}$ consists of the disks whose radii lie between $2^{i-1}$ and $2^i$. By the discussion above, the expected number of disks intersected by a random line through an arbitrary point $p$ is $O(\sqrt{(m_i+n_i)\log n_i})$, where $n_i=|{\cal D}_i|$ and $m_i$ is the number of intersecting pairs of disks in ${\cal D}_i$. Therefore, such a random line intersects $O(\sum_{i=1}^{\lceil \log_2\Delta\rceil} \sqrt{(m_i+n_i) \log n_i})$ disks in $\cal{D}$ in expectation. Note that \[ \sum_{i=1}^{\lceil \log_2\Delta\rceil} \sqrt{(m_i+n_i) \log n_i}) = O(\sqrt{(m+n)\log n}\log \Delta), \] where $n=|\cal{D}|$ and $m$ is the number of intersecting pairs of disks in $\cal{D}$. By choosing a centerpoint of disk centers as $p$, we obtain the following corollary.
nodes.statement_short: Group disks into $\lceil\log_2\Delta\rceil$ radius classes within factor 2, apply the bounded-radii lemma per class and sum; take $p$ a centerpoint.
