nodes.name: Minimum of sum of pair counts under fixed total
nodes.statement: Let $n,k$ be positive integers, and $f(x_1, \dots, x_k) = \sum_{i=1}^k x_i(x_i-1)/2$. Then, $\min\{f(x_1, \dots, x_k) \mid (x_1,\dots,x_k) \in \mathbb{Z}^k, \sum_{i=1}^k x_i = n\} \geq n^2/(2k) - n/2$.
assumptions: Let $n,k$ be positive integers
conclusions: $\min\{f(x_1, \dots, x_k) \mid (x_1,\dots,x_k) \in \mathbb{Z}^k, \sum_{i=1}^k x_i = n\} \geq n^2/(2k) - n/2$
nodes.statement_short: Splitting $n$ items into $k$ groups yields at least $n^2/(2k)-n/2$ within-group pairs.
nodes.label: lem:uniform

nodes.name: Proof of Theorem (axis-parallel separator)
nodes.statement: Let $P$ be the set of disk centers and assume that there are no two points (centers) in $P$ with the same $x$-coordinate or the same $y$-coordinate. Let $\ell_d$ (resp., $\ell_u$) be a horizontal line such that there are exactly $n/5$ points of $P$ below it (resp., above it). Let $H$ be the distance between~$\ell_d$ and~$\ell_u$. Similarly, let $\ell_l$ (resp., $\ell_r$) be a vertical line such that there are exactly $n/5$ points of $P$ to its left (resp., to its right). Let $V$ be the distance between $\ell_l$ and $\ell_r$. {From} the above definitions, it follows that any horizontal line $\ell$ between $\ell_d$ and $\ell_u$, and any vertical line $\ell$ between $\ell_l$ and $\ell_r$ have at most $4n/5$ disks of $\cal{D}$ on each of the two open halfplanes bounded by $\ell$. We will show that one of these lines intersects $O(\sqrt{m+n})$ disks of $\cal{D}$. Consider the rectangle $\cal{R}$ defined by $\ell_d$, $\ell_u$, $\ell_l$ and $\ell_r$. Now let $h_i$ be the horizontal line above $\ell_d$ whose distance from $\ell_d$ is exactly $i$, for $i=1,\ldots,\lceil H-1\rceil$, and similarly, let $v_i$ be the vertical line to the right of $\ell_l$ whose distance from $\ell_l$ is exactly $i$, for $i=1,\ldots,\lceil V-1 \rceil$. We have a case analysis. Assume first that $H < 2$ and $V<2$. Then, there exist a horizontal line between $\ell_d$ and $\ell_u$, and a vertical line between $\ell_l$ and $\ell_r$ that intersect at least $n/5$ disks whose centers are in $\cal{R}$. What we need to show is $m=\Omega(n^2)$ as any line intersects at most $O(n)$ disks. We partition $\cal{R}$ into at most $4$ rectangles by $h_i$ and $v_i$ so that each side of these rectangles is at most $\sqrt{2}$. By Lemma~\ref{lem:uniform} with $k \leq 4$, we have $m \geq n^2/200 - n/10 = \Omega(n^2)$. Next we assume that $H \geq 2$ and $V \geq 2$. Then, no disk with center below $\ell_d$ or above $\ell_u$ (resp., left to $\ell_l$ or right to $\ell_r$) intersects $h_i$ for $i=1, \ldots, \lfloor H-1 \rfloor$ (resp., $v_i$ for $i=1, \ldots, \lfloor V-1 \rfloor$). The number of centers in $\cal{R}$ is at least $n/5$ and any disk whose center is in $\cal{R}$ is intersected by at most three of the horizontal lines $h_i$ and by at most three of the vertical lines $v_i$. Now, if one (or more) of the lines $h_i$ or one (or more) of the lines $v_i$ intersects at most $\lambda \sqrt{m+n/10}$ disks, for some constant $\lambda$ that we specify below, then we are done. Assume therefore that each of the lines $h_i$ and each of the lines $v_i$ intersects more than $\lambda \sqrt{m+n/10}$ disks. Since no disk with center below $\ell_d$ or above $\ell_u$ (resp., left to $\ell_l$ or right to $\ell_r$) intersects $h_i$ for $i=1, \ldots, \lfloor H-1 \rfloor$ (resp., $v_j$ for $j=1, \ldots, \lfloor V-1 \rfloor$), we have \[ \lambda \sqrt{m+n/10} \lfloor H-1 \rfloor \leq 3\left(\frac{3n}{5}\right), \quad \text{and} \quad \lambda \sqrt{m+n/10} \lfloor V-1 \rfloor \leq 3\left(\frac{3n}{5}\right); \] otherwise we get that the number of disks is greater than $n$. We partition $\cal{R}$ into $N$ rectangles using $h_i$ and $v_j$ for $1 \leq i \leq \lceil H-1 \rceil$ and $1 \leq j \leq \lceil V-1 \rceil$ so that each side of these rectangles is at most $\sqrt{2}$. Then, the disk centers in $\cal{R}$ are distributed into $N$ rectangles, and the disks with centers in the same rectangle form a clique. Let $x_i$ be the number of centers in one of the $N$ rectangles, for $i=1,\ldots, N$, where $\sum_{i=1}^N x_i \geq n/5$. By Lemma~\ref{lem:uniform} with $k=N$, the number of intersecting pairs of disks whose centers lie in $\cal{R}$ is at least $n^2/(50N) - n/10$. Then, we have \[ m + \frac{n}{10} \geq \frac{n^2}{50N}. \] On the other hand, we have \[ N = \lceil H \rceil \lceil V \rceil \leq (\lfloor H -1 \rfloor + 2) (\lfloor V -1 \rfloor + 2) \leq 9 (\lfloor H -1 \rfloor) (\lfloor V -1 \rfloor) \leq 81 \left(\frac{3n}{5}\right)^2 \cdot \frac{1}{\lambda^2 (m+n/10)}. \] Therefore, we conclude that \[ m + \frac{n}{10} \geq \frac{n^2}{50} \cdot \frac{25}{729n^2} \cdot \lambda^2 \left(m+\frac{n}{10}\right) = \frac{1}{1458} \lambda^2 \left(m+\frac{n}{10}\right) > m+\frac{n}{10}, \] assuming $\lambda > \sqrt{1458}$. This is a contradiction. Finally we assume that $H \geq 2$ and $V < 2$ (the case where $V \geq 2$ and $H < 2$ is symmetric). We argue as in the previous case. If one (or more) of the lines $h_i$ intersects at most $\lambda \sqrt{m+n/10}$ disks, for some constant $\lambda$ that we specify below, then we are done. Assume therefore that each of the lines $h_i$ intersects more than $\lambda \sqrt{m+n/10}$ disks. Then, we have \[ \lambda \sqrt{m+n/10} \lfloor H-1 \rfloor \leq 3\left(\frac{3n}{5}\right), \] and if we partition $\cal{R}$ into $N$ rectangles using $h_i$ and $v_j$ for $1 \leq i \leq \lceil H-1 \rceil$ and $j \leq \lceil V-1 \rceil$ so that each side of these rectangles is at most $\sqrt{2}$, then we have \[ N \leq 2 \lceil H \rceil \leq 2 (\lfloor H -1 \rfloor + 2) \leq 6 (\lfloor H -1 \rfloor) \leq \frac{54n}{5\lambda\sqrt{m+n/10}}. \] Again, as in the previous case, we have \[ m + \frac{n}{10} \geq \frac{n^2}{50N} \geq \frac{n^2}{50} \cdot \frac{5 \lambda \sqrt{m+\dfrac{n}{10}}}{54n} > \frac{\lambda\sqrt{2}}{540} \cdot \frac{n \sqrt{m+\dfrac{n}{10}}}{\sqrt{2}} > \frac{\sqrt{2}\lambda}{540} \left(m +\frac{n}{10}\right) > m+\frac{n}{10}, \] assuming $\lambda > 540/\sqrt{2}$. The second to last inequality follows from the upper bound on $m$ in the complete graph, i.e.\ $m \leq n(n-1)/2 \Rightarrow \sqrt{m+n/10} < n/\sqrt{2}$. Thus, we have reached a contradiction. \qed
nodes.statement_short: Take quintile lines in $x$ and $y$; case analysis on the rectangle's side lengths, with unit-spaced lines and the pair-count lemma forcing $m=\Omega(\cdot)$ if every line is heavy. Contradiction with constant $\lambda$ large.

nodes.name: Almost tightness of the centerpoint approach
nodes.statement: For any $n,m\in \mathbb{N}$ such that $9n \leq m \leq \lfloor n^2/6 \rfloor$, there exist $n', m' \in \mathbb{N}$, where $n \leq n' \leq 2n$ and $\lceil m/9 \rceil \leq m' \leq 6m$, and a set $\cal{D}$ of $n'$ unit disks in the plane with $m'$ intersecting pairs that have the following property. There exists a centerpoint $p$ of the centers of unit disks in $\cal{D}$ such that any line $\ell$ that passes through $p$ intersects $\Omega( \sqrt{m\log (n/\sqrt{m})})$ disks of $\cal{D}$.
assumptions: For any $n,m\in \mathbb{N}$ such that $9n \leq m \leq \lfloor n^2/6 \rfloor$
conclusions: there exist $n', m' \in \mathbb{N}$, where $n \leq n' \leq 2n$ and $\lceil m/9 \rceil \leq m' \leq 6m$, and a set $\cal{D}$ of $n'$ unit disks in the plane with $m'$ intersecting pairs that have the following property
There exists a centerpoint $p$ of the centers of unit disks in $\cal{D}$ such that any line $\ell$ that passes through $p$ intersects $\Omega( \sqrt{m\log (n/\sqrt{m})})$ disks of $\cal{D}$.
nodes.statement_short: There are unit-disk families with a centerpoint through which every line meets $\Omega(\sqrt{m\log(n/\sqrt m)})$ disks.
nodes.label: thm:lowerjoint_unit

nodes.name: Proof of Theorem (almost tightness)
nodes.statement: Given $n$ and $m$ we choose $k\in \mathbb{N}$ as the smallest natural number $k'$ such that $k' \geq \sqrt{\frac{{6m}}{{1+\ln (n/k')}}}$. First observe that such $k$ exists and satisfies $k\leq n$. Indeed, let $f(x)=\sqrt{\frac{6m}{1+\ln{(n/x)}}}$. Since $f(x)$ is monotonically increasing for $x \geq 1$, it suffices to show that $n-f(n) \geq 0$. This holds as $$ n-f(n) \geq 0 \Leftrightarrow n-\sqrt{6m} \geq 0 \Leftrightarrow n^2/6 \geq m,$$ and the last inequality is true by our assumed bounds on $m$. Let $\ell=\lceil n/k \rceil$, and consider a sufficiently small positive real number \mbox{$\varepsilon \leq \frac{1}{2\pi}$}. Consider now the $\ell$ concentric circles $C_i$ centered at the origin with radius \mbox{$2i(1+\varepsilon)$} for $i=1, \dots, \ell$. On each such circle, we place $k$ unit disks uniformly (i.e., the arc spacing between the centers of two consecutive disks is $4\pi i(1+\varepsilon)/k$). Let $\cal{D}$ be the collection of these disks, see \figurename~\ref{fig:lowerBound}, left. Let $n' = k\ell$. By construction, $\cal{D}$ has $n'$ disks, and $n \leq n' \leq n+k \leq 2n$ as claimed. Partition the disks of $\cal{D}$ into $\ell$ layers ${\cal D}_1, \dots, {\cal D}_{\ell}$ depending on which concentric circle their center lies on. Since we placed unit disks on circles that are $2(1+\varepsilon)$ units apart, only disks that belong to the same layer may have nonempty intersection. We now show that the number $m'$ of intersecting pairs in $\cal{D}$ satisfies $\lceil m/9 \rceil \leq m' \leq 6m$. Let $x_i$ denote the number of intersecting pairs of disks on the $i$-th layer, and let $\gamma_i$ be the arc length of $C_i$ such that two unit disks centered at two endpoints of the arc touch each other (see \figurename~\ref{fig:lowerBound}, middle). Note that two disks on the same layer overlap if and only if the arc distance between the centers is $\gamma_i$ or less, and disks in different layers cannot intersect. Since the disks are evenly spaced on $C_i$, each disk of ${\cal D}_i$ intersects $2\lfloor \frac{\gamma_i}{4\pi i(1+\varepsilon)/k} \rfloor $ other disks. Taking into account that there are $k$ disks in ${\cal D}_i$ (and each crossing is counted twice), we obtain that $x_i= \lfloor\frac{\gamma_ik}{4\pi i(1+\varepsilon)}\rfloor k$ and thus the total number of intersecting pairs is $m'=\sum_{i=1}^{\ell} x_i = \sum_{i=1}^{\ell} \lfloor\frac{\gamma_ik}{4\pi i(1+\varepsilon)}\rfloor k$. By using some trigonometric properties and picking a sufficiently small $\varepsilon$, we can show that, regardless of the value of $i$, we have $$2 < \gamma_i = 4i(1+\varepsilon)\sin^{-1}(1/2i(1+\varepsilon)) < 2\pi/3.$$ We now bound $m'$ from above. Since $\gamma_i< 2\pi/3$, we have $$m' < \sum_{i=1}^{\ell} \frac{ k^2}{6 i(1+\varepsilon)} < \frac{k^2}{6}\sum_{i=1}^{\ell} \frac{1}{i} < k^2(1+\ln \ell)/6 < k^2(1+\ln (2n/k))/6.$$ Recall that we choose $k$ to be the smallest natural number $k'$ such that $k' \geq \sqrt{\frac{{6m}}{{1+\ln (n/k')}}}$. We combine this bound with the assumption that $n<m$ to obtain the desired bound: \begin{align*} m' &< k^2\frac{(1+\ln (2n/k))}{6} < \left(1+\sqrt{\frac{{6m}}{{1+\ln (n/k)}}}\right)^2 \left(\sqrt{\frac{(1+2\ln (n/k))}{6}}\right)^2 \\ &< \left(\sqrt{\frac{1+2\ln (n/k)}{6}}+\sqrt{2m} \right)^2 <\left(\sqrt{\frac{6n}{6}}+\sqrt{2m} \right)^2 \\ &< (\sqrt{m}+\sqrt{2m})^2 =(3+2\sqrt{2}) m. \end{align*} For the lower bound we now use that $\gamma_i>2$ (and $\varepsilon \leq \frac{1}{2\pi}$). Recall that \begin{align*} m' &= \sum_{i=1}^{\ell} \left\lfloor\frac{\gamma_ik}{4\pi i(1+\varepsilon)}\right\rfloor k > \sum_{i=1}^{\ell} \left( \frac{k}{2\pi i(1+\varepsilon)} -1\right) k > \frac{k^2}{2\pi + 1} \left(\sum_{i=1}^{\ell} \frac{1}{i}\right) - \left(\sum_{i=1}^{\ell} k\right) > \frac{k^2 \ln(l+1)}{2\pi + 1} - n'. \end{align*} Recall that, by choice of $k$, we have $k \geq \sqrt{\frac{{6m}}{{1+\ln (n/k)}}}$ and in particular $k \geq \sqrt{\frac{6m}{1+\ln \ell}}$. Combining this fact with $\ln(\ell+1) \geq (1+\ln \ell)/2$ and $2m/9 \geq n'$ gives us the lower bound as follows: $$ m' \geq \left(\frac{6m}{1+\ln \ell }\right) \left(\frac{\ln(\ell+1)}{2\pi + 1}\right) - n' \geq \frac{3m}{2\pi + 1} - \frac{2m}{9} > \frac{3m}{9} - \frac{2m}{9}=\frac{m}{9}. $$ That is, for any values of $n$ and $m \in \{9n,\dots,\lfloor n^2/6 \rfloor\}$, we can construct a set of $n'$ unit disks with $m'$ intersecting pairs. By symmetry, we can see that the origin is a centerpoint of the centers of disks in $\cal{D}$. Thus, it remains to show that any line that passes through the origin must intersect many disks of ${\cal D}$. In the following we show something stronger: any ray emanating from a point $p$ inside $C_1$ will cross $\Omega( \sqrt{m\log (n/\sqrt{m})})$ disks. We count the number of intersections on each layer independently. Each unit disk in ${\cal D}_i$ covers $\frac{\gamma_i}{2i(1+\varepsilon)}$ radians of $C_i$. Since there are $k$ evenly spread disks in ${\cal D}_i$ and $\varepsilon \leq \frac{1}{4\pi}$, each point of the circle $C_i$ is contained in at least $\lfloor \frac{\gamma_i k}{2i(1+\varepsilon)} \cdot \frac{1}{2\pi} \rfloor > \frac{\gamma_i k}{i(4\pi +1)} - 1$ disks. By substituting $k \geq \sqrt{\frac{6m}{1+\ln \ell}}$, $\gamma_i > 2$, $\ln(\ell+1) \geq (1+\ln \ell)/2$, $\ell = n'/k$ and $2m/9 \geq n'$, we obtain that the number of disks in ${\cal D}$ intersected by the ray is at least \begin{align*} \sum_{i=1}^{\ell} (\frac{\gamma_i k}{i(4\pi +1)} - 1) & > \frac{2}{4\pi + 1}\left(\sqrt{\frac{6m}{1+\ln \ell }}\right)\left( \sum_{i=1}^{\ell} \frac{1}{i}\right) - \ell\\ & \geq \frac{2}{4\pi + 1} \left(\sqrt{\frac{6m}{1+\ln \ell}}\right)\ln(\ell +1) - \frac{n' \sqrt{1+\ln \ell}}{\sqrt{6m}}\\ & \geq \frac{\sqrt{6m (1+\ln \ell )}}{4\pi + 1} - \frac{2m}{9} \sqrt{\frac{1+\ln \ell}{6m}}\\ & \geq \left(\frac{\sqrt{6}}{4\pi + 1} - \frac{2}{9\sqrt{6}}\right) \sqrt{m(1+\ln \ell)} = \Omega( \sqrt{m\log (n/\sqrt{m})}). \tag*{\qed} \end{align*}
nodes.statement_short: Construction: $k$ evenly spaced unit disks on each of $\ell$ concentric circles of radius $2i(1+\varepsilon)$. Bounding $m'$ via harmonic sums and counting disk coverage of each circle shows every ray from the center meets $\Omega(\sqrt{m\log(n/\sqrt m)})$ disks.

nodes.name: No sublinear line separator for disks of arbitrary radii
nodes.statement: For any $n\in \mathbb{N}$ there exists a set $\cal{D}$ of $O(n)$ pairwise disjoint disks such that any line $\ell$ for which both halfplanes contain $\Omega(n)$ disks of $\cal{D}$ also intersects $\Omega(n)$ disks of $\cal{D}$.
assumptions: For any $n\in \mathbb{N}$
conclusions: there exists a set $\cal{D}$ of $O(n)$ pairwise disjoint disks such that any line $\ell$ for which both halfplanes contain $\Omega(n)$ disks of $\cal{D}$ also intersects $\Omega(n)$ disks of $\cal{D}$
nodes.label: thm:lowerarbitRad

nodes.name: Proof of Theorem (arbitrary radii lower bound)
nodes.statement: Our construction is similar to the one of Theorem~\ref{thm:lowerjoint_unit}: let ${\cal C}_1$ be the set containing the unit disk centered at the origin. For $i>1$, let $D_i$ be the smallest enclosing disk containing all disks of ${\cal C}_{i-1}$. The set ${\cal C}_i$ (for $i>1$) is defined as the set containing the six disks of the same radius as $D_i$ surrounding $D_i$, such that each two consecutive disks touch and none overlap. Note that $D_i\not\in {\cal C}_{i}$ and ${\cal C}=\bigcup_{i=1}^n {\cal C}_i$. Observe that in this construction disks of one level touch only neighbors on the same level (and on the next and previous level). We fix this by rotating the construction so that disks in ${\cal C}_i$ are tangent to $D_i$ but do not intersect with the disks of ${\cal C}_{i-1}$ (see Figure~\ref{fig:lowerBound} right). Tangencies can afterwards be removed by shirking the disks by a factor of $1-\varepsilon$ for a sufficiently small value of $\varepsilon$. We also shrink the disk in ${\cal C}_1$ by this factor of $1-\varepsilon$. After these two changes the disks will be pairwise disjoint. The argument is now similar to the one in Theorem~\ref{thm:lowerjoint_unit}, and the centers of the disks in $\cal C$ are placed in concentric circles around the origin. The main difference now is that each layer has a constant number of disks. Thus, any line $\ell$ that makes a balanced separator must cross $\Omega(n)$ concentric circles. For every two intersections we can find at least one disk that intersects with $\ell$, and thus the $\Omega(n)$ lower bound follows. \qed
nodes.statement_short: Nested construction of six disks of exponentially growing radius around each enclosing disk, so a balanced line must cross $\Omega(n)$ layers.

nodes.name: Near-optimality of the arbitrary-radii bound
nodes.statement: Note that in this construction the radii of the disks grow at an exponential rate. Therefore, our upper bound in Corollary \ref{cor:arb_radii} is nearly optimal also in this sense.
nodes.statement_short: Radii grow exponentially in the lower-bound construction, so the $\log\Delta$ factor of the arbitrary-radii corollary is nearly optimal.

nodes.name: Centerpoint random-line separator algorithm
nodes.statement: Theorem~\ref{thm:joint_unit} suggests a simple algorithm: find a centerpoint (which can be done in linear time~\cite{DBLP:journals/dcg/JadhavM94}) and try random lines passing through that point until a good separator is found.
nodes.statement_short: Compute a centerpoint and try random lines through it until a good separator appears.

nodes.name: Random-slope minimum 2/3-separator algorithm
nodes.statement: Since implementing the centerpoint algorithm is not trivial, we use an alternative method that is asymptotically slower but much easier to implement: for a slope $a$ selected uniformly at random find a $2/3$-separator with slope $a$ that intersects the minimum number of disks (this step can be done in $O(n \log n)$ time by sorting the disks in orthogonal direction of $a$ and making a plane sweep). Clearly, a separator found by the modified algorithm intersects at most as many disks as the line of the same slope passing through a centerpoint. Thus, as in Theorem~\ref{thm:joint_unit}, a random direction will be good with positive probability. We repeat this process many times to obtain a good line separator.
nodes.statement_short: Repeatedly pick a random slope and, by sorting and a sweep, take the $2/3$-separator of that slope crossing fewest disks.

nodes.name: Modified algorithm is no worse than the centerpoint line
nodes.statement: Clearly, a separator found by the modified algorithm intersects at most as many disks as the line of the same slope passing through a centerpoint.
conclusions: a separator found by the modified algorithm intersects at most as many disks as the line of the same slope passing through a centerpoint

nodes.name: A random direction is good with positive probability
nodes.statement: Thus, as in Theorem~\ref{thm:joint_unit}, a random direction will be good with positive probability.
conclusions: a random direction will be good with positive probability

nodes.name: Fox--Pach separator method
nodes.statement: First, we build the arrangement of curves, and obtain a plane graph whose vertex set are the vertices of the arrangement and consecutive vertices on a curve are joined by an edge.\footnote{The method of Fox and Pach needs to add a constant number of additional vertices, but the main feature is that the overall complexity of the graph is $O(m+n)$.} We triangulate the obtained plane graph to make it maximal planar. Then, we find a simple cycle $2/3$-separator $C$ (i.e., a $2/3$-separator that forms a cycle in the graph) of size $O(\sqrt{m+n})$, which always exists \cite{DBLP:journals/jcss/Miller86}. We output all curves containing a vertex in $C$.
nodes.section: 4.1 The Method by Fox and Pach
output: all curves containing a vertex in $C$
nodes.statement_short: Build the curve arrangement as a plane graph, triangulate it, find an $O(\sqrt{m+n})$ simple cycle $2/3$-separator, and output curves touching it.

nodes.name: random instance
nodes.statement: Random instances are generated at random, as usually done for the experimental work on sensor networks. We fix a square $S$ of side length $L$ and generate $n$ unit disks in $S$ independently and uniformly at random. If the graph is disconnected, we discard it and generate again.
nodes.statement_short: $n$ unit disks placed independently uniformly at random in a square of side $L$, resampled until the graph is connected.

nodes.name: Snake instance has a constant-size separator
nodes.statement: A particular trait of this instance is that it has a separator of constant size: a vertical line can do a balanced cut and only intersect one disk.
conclusions: it has a separator of constant size: a vertical line can do a balanced cut and only intersect one disk

nodes.name: snake instance
nodes.statement: The specific construction of the snake instance is as follows: for ease of generation, we set the radius of the unit disks to $4/3$, and we fix an odd integer $q$. Let $n=(q^2-1)/2 + q$. We place $n$ unit disk centers at integer coordinates $(x,y) \in \{2i-1 \mid 1\leq i \leq (q+1)/2\} \times \{j \mid 1\leq j \leq q\} \cup \{(2i, q^{i \bmod 2}) \mid 1\leq i\leq (q-1)/2 \}$. Note that $q^{i \bmod 2}$ is equal to $1$ when $i$ is even, and is equal to $q$ when $i$ is odd. Hence, for each $q$, the snake instance is uniquely determined.
nodes.statement_short: For odd $q$, $n=(q^2-1)/2+q$ disks of radius $4/3$ on odd columns of a $q$-grid joined alternately at top and bottom, forming a path.

nodes.name: Edge count of the snake instance
nodes.statement: Observe that, by constructions, the number $m$ of edges is $n-1 = (q^2-1)/2 + q-1$.
conclusions: the number $m$ of edges is $n-1 = (q^2-1)/2 + q-1$

nodes.name: optimal line separator
nodes.statement: Here, an \emph{optimal line separator} means the line that intersects the fewest disks, that also is a $2/3$-separator.
nodes.section: 4.4 Experiment 2: Comparison with the Method by Fox and Pach

nodes.name: Optimal line separator in near-quadratic time
nodes.statement: Such a line can be found in $\tilde{O}(n^2)$ time by looking at all possible bitangents and finding the best $2/3$-separator among those that have that fixed direction, where the $\tilde{O}(\cdot)$ notation suppresses logarithmic factors.
nodes.section: 4.4 Experiment 2: Comparison with the Method by Fox and Pach
conclusions: Such a line can be found in $\tilde{O}(n^2)$ time

nodes.name: Empirical Theta(sqrt m) separator size
nodes.statement: However, the experiments show something more interesting: the size of the separator seems to have an asymptotic $\Theta( \sqrt{m})$ behavior. This further pushes our intuition that the upper bound of Theorem~\ref{thm:joint_unit} is loose.
nodes.section: 4.3 Experiment 1: Quality of the Proposed Method
nodes.statement_short: Experiments suggest separator size grows like $\Theta(\sqrt m)$, hinting the $\sqrt{\log n}$ factor of the theorem is loose.

nodes.name: Line separators beat Fox--Pach on random instances
nodes.statement: On average, our method is strictly better than the Fox-Pach method even when $k=1$ (that is, both methods provide a $2/3$-separator, but ours intersects fewer disks).
nodes.section: 4.4 Experiment 2: Comparison with the Method by Fox and Pach

nodes.name: Better balance for line separators
nodes.statement: It is an open problem to give a better bound on the balance of a line separator, possibly at the expense of a worse bound on the separator size.

nodes.name: Extension to fat convex objects of similar size
nodes.statement: The method explained at the end of Section \ref{subsec:generalcase} can be used to show a similar result to Theorem~\ref{thm:joint_unit} for \emph{fat} convex objects of similar size \cite{DBLP:journals/algorithmica/BergSVK02}.
conclusions: can be used to show a similar result to Theorem~\ref{thm:joint_unit} for \emph{fat} convex objects of similar size

nodes.name: Line separators for arbitrary convex objects of similar size
nodes.statement: However, we do not know whether the method can be extended to arbitrary convex objects of similar size. This is another open problem.

nodes.name: Concentric circles around p
nodes.statement: Let $C_i$ be the circle of radius $2i$ centered at $p$, for $i=0,1,\ldots$. Then each disk in ${\cal D}$ is intersected by at most two of these circles---if a disk is intersected by two circles the intersection takes place on the boundary of the disk.
nodes.statement_short: Introduce circles $C_i$ of radius $2i$; each disk meets at most two.

nodes.name: Layers D_i
nodes.statement: Let ${\cal D}_i \subseteq {\cal D}$ be the set of disks that have non-empty intersection with $C_i$, for $i=0,1,\ldots$. See \figurename~\ref{fig:disjoint_unit}. Note that $\sum_{i} |{\cal D}_i| \leq 2n$.
nodes.statement_short: Define layers ${\cal D}_i$ with $\sum_i|{\cal D}_i|\le 2n$.

nodes.name: Figure float inside the proof
nodes.statement: \begin{figure}[t] \centering \begin{minipage}{0.31\textwidth} \centering \resizebox{\textwidth}{!}{\includegraphics{disjoint_unit}} \caption{Proof of Lemma \ref{lem:disjoint_unit}. The number $i$ in each disk means that it intersects the circle of radius $2i$ centered at $p$. } \end{minipage} \hfill \begin{minipage}{0.64\textwidth} \centering \resizebox{\textwidth}{!}{\includegraphics{joint_unit}} \caption{Proof of Lemma \ref{lem:joint_unit}. (a) A grid of $\sqrt{2}\times \sqrt{2}$ squares is laid over the family of unit disks. (b) Disks associated to the same cell intersect, but disks associated to different cells of the same color do not intersect. If $j$ is the index for color yellow, then $n_j = 7$, $l_{j0}=4$, and $l_{j1}=1$ in this example.} \end{minipage} \end{figure}
nodes.statement_short: Figure float (Figures 2 and 3) placed inside the proof; not part of the argument.

nodes.name: Caption item (a)
nodes.statement: (a) A grid of $\sqrt{2}\times \sqrt{2}$ squares is laid over the family of unit disks.
nodes.statement_short: Caption panel (a): grid laid over the disks.

nodes.name: Caption item (b)
nodes.statement: (b) Disks associated to the same cell intersect, but disks associated to different cells of the same color do not intersect. If $j$ is the index for color yellow, then $n_j = 7$, $l_{j0}=4$, and $l_{j1}=1$ in this example.}
nodes.statement_short: Caption panel (b): coloring of grid cells.

nodes.name: Per-layer expectation
nodes.statement: Given a random line $\ell$ through $p$, the number $k_i$ of disks of ${\cal D}_i$ that are intersected by $\ell$ is at most four, due to disjointness, and its expectation is $O(|{\cal D}_i|/i)$.
nodes.statement_short: A random line meets at most four disks of ${\cal D}_i$, expected $O(|{\cal D}_i|/i)$.

nodes.name: Sum over layers
nodes.statement: Therefore, by the linearity of expectation, the expected number of disks of $\cal{D}$ intersected by $\ell$ is bounded by \begin{align*} \mathbb{E}\left[\sum_{i \ge 0} k_i\right] &= \mathbb{E}\left[\sum_{i\colon i\leq \sqrt{n}} k_i\right] + \mathbb{E}\left[\sum_{i\colon i > \sqrt{n}} k_i\right]\\ &\le 4\sqrt{n} + \sum_{i\colon i > \sqrt{n}} O(|{\cal D}_i|/\sqrt{n}) = O(\sqrt{n}) + O(n/\sqrt{n}) = O(\sqrt{n}). \tag*{\qed} \end{align*}
nodes.statement_short: Split the sum at $i=\sqrt n$ to get $O(\sqrt n)$.

nodes.name: Line through a centerpoint
nodes.statement: Let $p$ be a centerpoint of the set of centers of disks in ${\cal D}$. By Lemma~\ref{lem:disjoint_unit}, some line through $p$ must intersect at most $O(\sqrt{n})$ disks from ${\cal D}$.
nodes.statement_short: Take a centerpoint $p$; by the lemma some line through it meets $O(\sqrt n)$ disks.

nodes.name: Balance from centerpoint
nodes.statement: Since $p$ is a centerpoint, each of the two open halfplanes bounded by $\ell$ contains at most $2n/3$ centers of disks in ${\cal D}$, which means that the halfplane contains at most $2n/3$ disks from ${\cal D}$.
nodes.statement_short: Each open halfplane contains at most $2n/3$ disks.

nodes.name: Randomized algorithm
nodes.statement: The argument above suggests the following algorithm: first we compute a centerpoint~$p$ of the centers of a given set of disks, and then choose a line through~$p$ uniformly at random.
nodes.statement_short: Algorithm: centerpoint, then a uniformly random line through it.

nodes.name: Markov bound on failure
nodes.statement: By Lemma \ref{lem:disjoint_unit} and Markov's inequality, the probability that the random line intersects more than $c\sqrt{n}$ disks is at most $1/4$ for some constant~$c$. Thus, a desired line can be found with probability at least $3/4$.
nodes.statement_short: Markov's inequality gives success probability at least $3/4$.

nodes.name: Running time
nodes.statement: The running time is linear in the number of disks since a centerpoint can be found in linear time \cite{DBLP:journals/dcg/JadhavM94}. \qed
nodes.statement_short: Linear time since a centerpoint is computable in linear time.

nodes.name: Grid of sqrt2 cells
nodes.statement: Consider a grid of $\sqrt{2} \times \sqrt{2}$ squares. Each grid cell is treated as right-open and top-open so that it is of the form of $[x,x+\sqrt{2})\times [y,y+\sqrt{2})$. Associate each disk in $\cal{D}$ with the grid cell containing its center, see \figurename~\ref{fig:joint_unit}(a).
nodes.statement_short: Assign each disk to the $\sqrt2\times\sqrt2$ grid cell of its center.

nodes.name: Nine-coloring
nodes.statement: Observe that one can color the grid cells with nine colors for every $3\times 3$ block of grid cells, so that no two disks that are associated with different grid cells of the same color intersect, see \figurename~\ref{fig:joint_unit}(b).
nodes.statement_short: Nine-color the cells so same-colored distinct cells hold non-intersecting disks.

nodes.name: Color classes C_j
nodes.statement: Consider one of the colors $j$, with $1 \le j \le 9$, and let ${\mathbb C}_j$ be the collection of subsets of $\cal{D}$ associated with the grid cells of this color: \[ {\mathbb C}_j = \{{\cal C} \subseteq {\cal D} \mid \text{ the center of disks in } {\cal C} \text{ lie in the same grid cell of color } j\}. \]
nodes.statement_short: Define ${\mathbb C}_j$, the cliques of cells of color $j$.

nodes.name: Clique and disjointness properties
nodes.statement: Then, ${\mathbb C}_j$ has the following two properties: (i) each subset ${\cal C} \in {\mathbb C}_j$ in the same grid cell is a clique, i.e., any two disks in the subset intersect each other; (ii) any two disks from two different subsets in ${\mathbb C}_j$ are pairwise disjoint.
nodes.statement_short: Each subset is a clique; different subsets are disjoint.

nodes.name: Buckets by clique size
nodes.statement: Let $n_j = \sum_{{\cal C} \in {\mathbb C}_j} |{\cal C}|$ denote the number of disks in ${\cal D}$ associated to grid cells of color $j$. We divide the cliques in ${\mathbb C}_j$ into $O(\log n_j)$ buckets ${\mathbb B}_{j0},{\mathbb B}_{j1},\ldots$, where ${\mathbb B}_{ji}$ consists of all cliques of ${\mathbb C}_j$ whose size is in the range $[2^i,2^{i+1})$. Set $l_{ji} = |{\mathbb B}_{ji}|$, for $i=0,1,\ldots$.
nodes.statement_short: Define $n_j$ and bucket cliques of color $j$ by size in $[2^i,2^{i+1})$.

nodes.name: Bucket size sums
nodes.statement: Then, the sum $x_{ji}$ of the sizes of the cliques in ${\mathbb B}_{ji}$ is in the range $l_{ji}2^i \le x_{ji} < l_{ji}2^{i+1} $. We also know that $\sum_i x_{ji} = n_j$.
nodes.statement_short: Bound $x_{ji}$ by $l_{ji}2^i$ and $l_{ji}2^{i+1}$, with $\sum_i x_{ji}=n_j$.

nodes.name: Pair counts m_ji
nodes.statement: Let $m_{ji} = \sum_{{\cal C} \in \mathbb{B}_{ji}} |{\cal C}|(|{\cal C}|-1)/2$ denote the number of pairs of intersecting disks within ${\mathbb B}_{ji}$. Then, $l_{ji} (2^{2i-1}-2^{i-1}) \le m_{ji} < l_{ji} (2^{2i+1}-2^{i})$ and $\sum_i m_{ji} \le \sum_j \sum_i m_{ji} \leq m.$
nodes.statement_short: Bound the intersecting pairs $m_{ji}$ in each bucket.

nodes.name: Apply the disjoint lemma per bucket
nodes.statement: We first compute the expected number of disks in cliques of ${\mathbb B}_{ji}$ intersected by a random line through $p$. Since the union of the disks in each clique is contained in a disk of radius 2 such that these disks of radius 2 are disjoint, a random line through $p$ intersects only $O(\sqrt{l_{ji}})$ cliques of ${\mathbb B}_{ji}$ by Lemma~\ref{lem:disjoint_unit}, and therefore only $O(\sqrt{l_{ji}}2^{i+1})$ disks of~${\cal D}$. By the definition of ${\mathbb B}_{ji}$, we have $l_{ji}2^{2i-1} \leq m_{ji} + l_{ji} 2^{i-1} \leq m_{ji} + x_{ji}/2$. Thus, a random line through $p$ intersects $O(\sqrt{m_{ji} + x_{ji}})$ disks in expectation.
nodes.statement_short: Radius-2 hulls of cliques are disjoint; the disjoint lemma gives $O(\sqrt{m_{ji}+x_{ji}})$ expected disks.

nodes.name: Sum with Cauchy--Schwarz
nodes.statement: Then, by the linearity of expectation, we sum the numbers for all $j=1, \ldots, 9$ and $i = 0, \ldots, \log n_j$: \begin{eqnarray*} \sum_j \sum_i O(\sqrt{m_{ji} + x_{ji}}) &\leq& O\left(\sqrt{\sum_j \sum_i (m_{ji} + x_{ji})} \sqrt{\sum_j \sum_i 1}\right)\\ &\leq& O(\sqrt{(m+n)\log n}), \end{eqnarray*} where the first inequality follows from the Cauchy--Schwarz inequality. \qed
nodes.statement_short: Sum over $O(\log n)$ buckets and 9 colors using Cauchy--Schwarz.

nodes.name: Classify by radius
nodes.statement: We may also generalize the argument when the radii of the disks are arbitrary. Let $\cal{D}$ be a set of disks of arbitrary radii. Then, we classify the disks in $\cal{D}$ by their radii.
nodes.statement_short: Partition arbitrary-radius disks by radius.

nodes.name: Radius classes D_i
nodes.statement: By scaling, we assume that the smallest radius of the disks is one. Let $\Delta$ be the radius of a largest disk (or, before scaling, the ratio between the smallest and the largest radius of the disks). Then, for each $i = 1,2,\dots,\lceil \log_2 \Delta \rceil$, the set ${\cal D}_i \subseteq \cal{D}$ consists of the disks whose radii lie between $2^{i-1}$ and $2^i$.
nodes.statement_short: Normalize min radius 1, let $\Delta$ be max radius, classes ${\cal D}_i$ with radii in $[2^{i-1},2^i]$.

nodes.name: Apply bounded-radii bound per class
nodes.statement: By the discussion above, the expected number of disks intersected by a random line through an arbitrary point $p$ is $O(\sqrt{(m_i+n_i)\log n_i})$, where $n_i=|{\cal D}_i|$ and $m_i$ is the number of intersecting pairs of disks in ${\cal D}_i$. Therefore, such a random line intersects $O(\sum_{i=1}^{\lceil \log_2\Delta\rceil} \sqrt{(m_i+n_i) \log n_i})$ disks in $\cal{D}$ in expectation.
nodes.statement_short: Each class contributes $O(\sqrt{(m_i+n_i)\log n_i})$ in expectation.

nodes.name: Sum over classes
nodes.statement: Note that \[ \sum_{i=1}^{\lceil \log_2\Delta\rceil} \sqrt{(m_i+n_i) \log n_i}) = O(\sqrt{(m+n)\log n}\log \Delta), \] where $n=|\cal{D}|$ and $m$ is the number of intersecting pairs of disks in $\cal{D}$.
nodes.statement_short: The sum is $O(\sqrt{(m+n)\log n}\log\Delta)$.

nodes.name: Choose centerpoint
nodes.statement: By choosing a centerpoint of disk centers as $p$, we obtain the following corollary.
nodes.statement_short: Taking $p$ as a centerpoint yields the corollary.

nodes.name: Quintile lines
nodes.statement: Let $P$ be the set of disk centers and assume that there are no two points (centers) in $P$ with the same $x$-coordinate or the same $y$-coordinate. Let $\ell_d$ (resp., $\ell_u$) be a horizontal line such that there are exactly $n/5$ points of $P$ below it (resp., above it). Let $H$ be the distance between~$\ell_d$ and~$\ell_u$. Similarly, let $\ell_l$ (resp., $\ell_r$) be a vertical line such that there are exactly $n/5$ points of $P$ to its left (resp., to its right). Let $V$ be the distance between $\ell_l$ and $\ell_r$.
nodes.statement_short: Define quintile lines $\ell_d,\ell_u,\ell_l,\ell_r$ and their distances $H,V$.

nodes.name: Balance of lines in between
nodes.statement: {From} the above definitions, it follows that any horizontal line $\ell$ between $\ell_d$ and $\ell_u$, and any vertical line $\ell$ between $\ell_l$ and $\ell_r$ have at most $4n/5$ disks of $\cal{D}$ on each of the two open halfplanes bounded by $\ell$. We will show that one of these lines intersects $O(\sqrt{m+n})$ disks of $\cal{D}$.
nodes.statement_short: Any line between the quintile lines is $4/5$-balanced; it remains to find a light one.

nodes.name: Rectangle and unit-spaced lines
nodes.statement: Consider the rectangle $\cal{R}$ defined by $\ell_d$, $\ell_u$, $\ell_l$ and $\ell_r$. Now let $h_i$ be the horizontal line above $\ell_d$ whose distance from $\ell_d$ is exactly $i$, for $i=1,\ldots,\lceil H-1\rceil$, and similarly, let $v_i$ be the vertical line to the right of $\ell_l$ whose distance from $\ell_l$ is exactly $i$, for $i=1,\ldots,\lceil V-1 \rceil$.
nodes.statement_short: Define rectangle ${\cal R}$ and unit-spaced lines $h_i$, $v_i$.

nodes.name: Case H<2 and V<2
nodes.statement: We have a case analysis. Assume first that $H < 2$ and $V<2$. Then, there exist a horizontal line between $\ell_d$ and $\ell_u$, and a vertical line between $\ell_l$ and $\ell_r$ that intersect at least $n/5$ disks whose centers are in $\cal{R}$. What we need to show is $m=\Omega(n^2)$ as any line intersects at most $O(n)$ disks. We partition $\cal{R}$ into at most $4$ rectangles by $h_i$ and $v_i$ so that each side of these rectangles is at most $\sqrt{2}$. By Lemma~\ref{lem:uniform} with $k \leq 4$, we have $m \geq n^2/200 - n/10 = \Omega(n^2)$.
nodes.statement_short: Small rectangle: the centers in it form at most 4 cliques, so $m=\Omega(n^2)$ by the lemma.

nodes.name: Case H>=2 and V>=2
nodes.statement: Next we assume that $H \geq 2$ and $V \geq 2$. Then, no disk with center below $\ell_d$ or above $\ell_u$ (resp., left to $\ell_l$ or right to $\ell_r$) intersects $h_i$ for $i=1, \ldots, \lfloor H-1 \rfloor$ (resp., $v_i$ for $i=1, \ldots, \lfloor V-1 \rfloor$). The number of centers in $\cal{R}$ is at least $n/5$ and any disk whose center is in $\cal{R}$ is intersected by at most three of the horizontal lines $h_i$ and by at most three of the vertical lines $v_i$. Now, if one (or more) of the lines $h_i$ or one (or more) of the lines $v_i$ intersects at most $\lambda \sqrt{m+n/10}$ disks, for some constant $\lambda$ that we specify below, then we are done. Assume therefore that each of the lines $h_i$ and each of the lines $v_i$ intersects more than $\lambda \sqrt{m+n/10}$ disks. Since no disk with center below $\ell_d$ or above $\ell_u$ (resp., left to $\ell_l$ or right to $\ell_r$) intersects $h_i$ for $i=1, \ldots, \lfloor H-1 \rfloor$ (resp., $v_j$ for $j=1, \ldots, \lfloor V-1 \rfloor$), we have \[ \lambda \sqrt{m+n/10} \lfloor H-1 \rfloor \leq 3\left(\frac{3n}{5}\right), \quad \text{and} \quad \lambda \sqrt{m+n/10} \lfloor V-1 \rfloor \leq 3\left(\frac{3n}{5}\right); \] otherwise we get that the number of disks is greater than $n$. We partition $\cal{R}$ into $N$ rectangles using $h_i$ and $v_j$ for $1 \leq i \leq \lceil H-1 \rceil$ and $1 \leq j \leq \lceil V-1 \rceil$ so that each side of these rectangles is at most $\sqrt{2}$. Then, the disk centers in $\cal{R}$ are distributed into $N$ rectangles, and the disks with centers in the same rectangle form a clique. Let $x_i$ be the number of centers in one of the $N$ rectangles, for $i=1,\ldots, N$, where $\sum_{i=1}^N x_i \geq n/5$. By Lemma~\ref{lem:uniform} with $k=N$, the number of intersecting pairs of disks whose centers lie in $\cal{R}$ is at least $n^2/(50N) - n/10$. Then, we have \[ m + \frac{n}{10} \geq \frac{n^2}{50N}. \] On the other hand, we have \[ N = \lceil H \rceil \lceil V \rceil \leq (\lfloor H -1 \rfloor + 2) (\lfloor V -1 \rfloor + 2) \leq 9 (\lfloor H -1 \rfloor) (\lfloor V -1 \rfloor) \leq 81 \left(\frac{3n}{5}\right)^2 \cdot \frac{1}{\lambda^2 (m+n/10)}. \] Therefore, we conclude that \[ m + \frac{n}{10} \geq \frac{n^2}{50} \cdot \frac{25}{729n^2} \cdot \lambda^2 \left(m+\frac{n}{10}\right) = \frac{1}{1458} \lambda^2 \left(m+\frac{n}{10}\right) > m+\frac{n}{10}, \] assuming $\lambda > \sqrt{1458}$. This is a contradiction.
nodes.statement_short: Both sides long: if every unit-spaced line is heavy, counting cliques gives a contradiction.

nodes.name: Case H>=2 and V<2
nodes.statement: Finally we assume that $H \geq 2$ and $V < 2$ (the case where $V \geq 2$ and $H < 2$ is symmetric). We argue as in the previous case. If one (or more) of the lines $h_i$ intersects at most $\lambda \sqrt{m+n/10}$ disks, for some constant $\lambda$ that we specify below, then we are done. Assume therefore that each of the lines $h_i$ intersects more than $\lambda \sqrt{m+n/10}$ disks. Then, we have \[ \lambda \sqrt{m+n/10} \lfloor H-1 \rfloor \leq 3\left(\frac{3n}{5}\right), \] and if we partition $\cal{R}$ into $N$ rectangles using $h_i$ and $v_j$ for $1 \leq i \leq \lceil H-1 \rceil$ and $j \leq \lceil V-1 \rceil$ so that each side of these rectangles is at most $\sqrt{2}$, then we have \[ N \leq 2 \lceil H \rceil \leq 2 (\lfloor H -1 \rfloor + 2) \leq 6 (\lfloor H -1 \rfloor) \leq \frac{54n}{5\lambda\sqrt{m+n/10}}. \] Again, as in the previous case, we have \[ m + \frac{n}{10} \geq \frac{n^2}{50N} \geq \frac{n^2}{50} \cdot \frac{5 \lambda \sqrt{m+\dfrac{n}{10}}}{54n} > \frac{\lambda\sqrt{2}}{540} \cdot \frac{n \sqrt{m+\dfrac{n}{10}}}{\sqrt{2}} > \frac{\sqrt{2}\lambda}{540} \left(m +\frac{n}{10}\right) > m+\frac{n}{10}, \] assuming $\lambda > 540/\sqrt{2}$. The second to last inequality follows from the upper bound on $m$ in the complete graph, i.e.\ $m \leq n(n-1)/2 \Rightarrow \sqrt{m+n/10} < n/\sqrt{2}$. Thus, we have reached a contradiction. \qed
nodes.statement_short: One long side: same argument with $N\le 2\lceil H\rceil$ cells, contradiction.

nodes.name: Lines avoid outside disks
nodes.statement: Next we assume that $H \geq 2$ and $V \geq 2$. Then, no disk with center below $\ell_d$ or above $\ell_u$ (resp., left to $\ell_l$ or right to $\ell_r$) intersects $h_i$ for $i=1, \ldots, \lfloor H-1 \rfloor$ (resp., $v_i$ for $i=1, \ldots, \lfloor V-1 \rfloor$). The number of centers in $\cal{R}$ is at least $n/5$ and any disk whose center is in $\cal{R}$ is intersected by at most three of the horizontal lines $h_i$ and by at most three of the vertical lines $v_i$.
nodes.statement_short: Lines $h_i,v_i$ meet only disks centered in ${\cal R}$, each at most three times.

nodes.name: Assume all lines heavy
nodes.statement: Now, if one (or more) of the lines $h_i$ or one (or more) of the lines $v_i$ intersects at most $\lambda \sqrt{m+n/10}$ disks, for some constant $\lambda$ that we specify below, then we are done. Assume therefore that each of the lines $h_i$ and each of the lines $v_i$ intersects more than $\lambda \sqrt{m+n/10}$ disks. Since no disk with center below $\ell_d$ or above $\ell_u$ (resp., left to $\ell_l$ or right to $\ell_r$) intersects $h_i$ for $i=1, \ldots, \lfloor H-1 \rfloor$ (resp., $v_j$ for $j=1, \ldots, \lfloor V-1 \rfloor$), we have \[ \lambda \sqrt{m+n/10} \lfloor H-1 \rfloor \leq 3\left(\frac{3n}{5}\right), \quad \text{and} \quad \lambda \sqrt{m+n/10} \lfloor V-1 \rfloor \leq 3\left(\frac{3n}{5}\right); \] otherwise we get that the number of disks is greater than $n$.
nodes.statement_short: Suppose every line meets more than $\lambda\sqrt{m+n/10}$ disks; bound $\lfloor H-1\rfloor$, $\lfloor V-1\rfloor$.

nodes.name: Cliques in cells
nodes.statement: We partition $\cal{R}$ into $N$ rectangles using $h_i$ and $v_j$ for $1 \leq i \leq \lceil H-1 \rceil$ and $1 \leq j \leq \lceil V-1 \rceil$ so that each side of these rectangles is at most $\sqrt{2}$. Then, the disk centers in $\cal{R}$ are distributed into $N$ rectangles, and the disks with centers in the same rectangle form a clique. Let $x_i$ be the number of centers in one of the $N$ rectangles, for $i=1,\ldots, N$, where $\sum_{i=1}^N x_i \geq n/5$. By Lemma~\ref{lem:uniform} with $k=N$, the number of intersecting pairs of disks whose centers lie in $\cal{R}$ is at least $n^2/(50N) - n/10$. Then, we have \[ m + \frac{n}{10} \geq \frac{n^2}{50N}. \]
nodes.statement_short: Partition into $N$ cells of side $\le\sqrt2$; the lemma gives $m+n/10\ge n^2/(50N)$.

nodes.name: Bound N
nodes.statement: On the other hand, we have \[ N = \lceil H \rceil \lceil V \rceil \leq (\lfloor H -1 \rfloor + 2) (\lfloor V -1 \rfloor + 2) \leq 9 (\lfloor H -1 \rfloor) (\lfloor V -1 \rfloor) \leq 81 \left(\frac{3n}{5}\right)^2 \cdot \frac{1}{\lambda^2 (m+n/10)}. \]
nodes.statement_short: Bound $N$ in terms of $\lambda$, $n$ and $m$.

nodes.name: Contradiction
nodes.statement: Therefore, we conclude that \[ m + \frac{n}{10} \geq \frac{n^2}{50} \cdot \frac{25}{729n^2} \cdot \lambda^2 \left(m+\frac{n}{10}\right) = \frac{1}{1458} \lambda^2 \left(m+\frac{n}{10}\right) > m+\frac{n}{10}, \] assuming $\lambda > \sqrt{1458}$. This is a contradiction.
nodes.statement_short: Combining yields a contradiction for $\lambda>\sqrt{1458}$.

nodes.name: Symmetric setup
nodes.statement: Finally we assume that $H \geq 2$ and $V < 2$ (the case where $V \geq 2$ and $H < 2$ is symmetric). We argue as in the previous case.
nodes.statement_short: Treat $H\ge2$, $V<2$ as in the previous case.

nodes.name: Assume all horizontal lines heavy
nodes.statement: If one (or more) of the lines $h_i$ intersects at most $\lambda \sqrt{m+n/10}$ disks, for some constant $\lambda$ that we specify below, then we are done. Assume therefore that each of the lines $h_i$ intersects more than $\lambda \sqrt{m+n/10}$ disks. Then, we have \[ \lambda \sqrt{m+n/10} \lfloor H-1 \rfloor \leq 3\left(\frac{3n}{5}\right), \] and if we partition $\cal{R}$ into $N$ rectangles using $h_i$ and $v_j$ for $1 \leq i \leq \lceil H-1 \rceil$ and $j \leq \lceil V-1 \rceil$ so that each side of these rectangles is at most $\sqrt{2}$, then we have \[ N \leq 2 \lceil H \rceil \leq 2 (\lfloor H -1 \rfloor + 2) \leq 6 (\lfloor H -1 \rfloor) \leq \frac{54n}{5\lambda\sqrt{m+n/10}}. \]
nodes.statement_short: If every $h_i$ is heavy, bound $\lfloor H-1\rfloor$ and the number $N$ of cells.

nodes.name: Contradiction
nodes.statement: Again, as in the previous case, we have \[ m + \frac{n}{10} \geq \frac{n^2}{50N} \geq \frac{n^2}{50} \cdot \frac{5 \lambda \sqrt{m+\dfrac{n}{10}}}{54n} > \frac{\lambda\sqrt{2}}{540} \cdot \frac{n \sqrt{m+\dfrac{n}{10}}}{\sqrt{2}} > \frac{\sqrt{2}\lambda}{540} \left(m +\frac{n}{10}\right) > m+\frac{n}{10}, \] assuming $\lambda > 540/\sqrt{2}$. The second to last inequality follows from the upper bound on $m$ in the complete graph, i.e.\ $m \leq n(n-1)/2 \Rightarrow \sqrt{m+n/10} < n/\sqrt{2}$. Thus, we have reached a contradiction. \qed
nodes.statement_short: The pair-count bound contradicts $\lambda>540/\sqrt2$.

nodes.name: Choose k
nodes.statement: Given $n$ and $m$ we choose $k\in \mathbb{N}$ as the smallest natural number $k'$ such that $k' \geq \sqrt{\frac{{6m}}{{1+\ln (n/k')}}}$.
nodes.statement_short: Choose $k$ minimal with $k\ge\sqrt{6m/(1+\ln(n/k))}$.

nodes.name: k exists and k<=n
nodes.statement: First observe that such $k$ exists and satisfies $k\leq n$. Indeed, let $f(x)=\sqrt{\frac{6m}{1+\ln{(n/x)}}}$. Since $f(x)$ is monotonically increasing for $x \geq 1$, it suffices to show that $n-f(n) \geq 0$. This holds as $$ n-f(n) \geq 0 \Leftrightarrow n-\sqrt{6m} \geq 0 \Leftrightarrow n^2/6 \geq m,$$ and the last inequality is true by our assumed bounds on $m$.
nodes.statement_short: Monotonicity of $f$ and $m\le n^2/6$ give $k\le n$.

nodes.name: Concentric construction
nodes.statement: Let $\ell=\lceil n/k \rceil$, and consider a sufficiently small positive real number \mbox{$\varepsilon \leq \frac{1}{2\pi}$}. Consider now the $\ell$ concentric circles $C_i$ centered at the origin with radius \mbox{$2i(1+\varepsilon)$} for $i=1, \dots, \ell$. On each such circle, we place $k$ unit disks uniformly (i.e., the arc spacing between the centers of two consecutive disks is $4\pi i(1+\varepsilon)/k$). Let $\cal{D}$ be the collection of these disks, see \figurename~\ref{fig:lowerBound}, left.
nodes.statement_short: Place $k$ unit disks evenly on each of $\ell$ circles of radius $2i(1+\varepsilon)$.

nodes.name: Number of disks
nodes.statement: Let $n' = k\ell$. By construction, $\cal{D}$ has $n'$ disks, and $n \leq n' \leq n+k \leq 2n$ as claimed.
nodes.statement_short: $n'=k\ell$ lies between $n$ and $2n$.

nodes.name: Layers
nodes.statement: Partition the disks of $\cal{D}$ into $\ell$ layers ${\cal D}_1, \dots, {\cal D}_{\ell}$ depending on which concentric circle their center lies on. Since we placed unit disks on circles that are $2(1+\varepsilon)$ units apart, only disks that belong to the same layer may have nonempty intersection.
nodes.statement_short: Only disks in the same layer can intersect.

nodes.name: Bounds on m'
nodes.statement: We now show that the number $m'$ of intersecting pairs in $\cal{D}$ satisfies $\lceil m/9 \rceil \leq m' \leq 6m$. Let $x_i$ denote the number of intersecting pairs of disks on the $i$-th layer, and let $\gamma_i$ be the arc length of $C_i$ such that two unit disks centered at two endpoints of the arc touch each other (see \figurename~\ref{fig:lowerBound}, middle). Note that two disks on the same layer overlap if and only if the arc distance between the centers is $\gamma_i$ or less, and disks in different layers cannot intersect. Since the disks are evenly spaced on $C_i$, each disk of ${\cal D}_i$ intersects $2\lfloor \frac{\gamma_i}{4\pi i(1+\varepsilon)/k} \rfloor $ other disks. Taking into account that there are $k$ disks in ${\cal D}_i$ (and each crossing is counted twice), we obtain that $x_i= \lfloor\frac{\gamma_ik}{4\pi i(1+\varepsilon)}\rfloor k$ and thus the total number of intersecting pairs is $m'=\sum_{i=1}^{\ell} x_i = \sum_{i=1}^{\ell} \lfloor\frac{\gamma_ik}{4\pi i(1+\varepsilon)}\rfloor k$. By using some trigonometric properties and picking a sufficiently small $\varepsilon$, we can show that, regardless of the value of $i$, we have $$2 < \gamma_i = 4i(1+\varepsilon)\sin^{-1}(1/2i(1+\varepsilon)) < 2\pi/3.$$ We now bound $m'$ from above. Since $\gamma_i< 2\pi/3$, we have $$m' < \sum_{i=1}^{\ell} \frac{ k^2}{6 i(1+\varepsilon)} < \frac{k^2}{6}\sum_{i=1}^{\ell} \frac{1}{i} < k^2(1+\ln \ell)/6 < k^2(1+\ln (2n/k))/6.$$ Recall that we choose $k$ to be the smallest natural number $k'$ such that $k' \geq \sqrt{\frac{{6m}}{{1+\ln (n/k')}}}$. We combine this bound with the assumption that $n<m$ to obtain the desired bound: \begin{align*} m' &< k^2\frac{(1+\ln (2n/k))}{6} < \left(1+\sqrt{\frac{{6m}}{{1+\ln (n/k)}}}\right)^2 \left(\sqrt{\frac{(1+2\ln (n/k))}{6}}\right)^2 \\ &< \left(\sqrt{\frac{1+2\ln (n/k)}{6}}+\sqrt{2m} \right)^2 <\left(\sqrt{\frac{6n}{6}}+\sqrt{2m} \right)^2 \\ &< (\sqrt{m}+\sqrt{2m})^2 =(3+2\sqrt{2}) m. \end{align*} For the lower bound we now use that $\gamma_i>2$ (and $\varepsilon \leq \frac{1}{2\pi}$). Recall that \begin{align*} m' &= \sum_{i=1}^{\ell} \left\lfloor\frac{\gamma_ik}{4\pi i(1+\varepsilon)}\right\rfloor k > \sum_{i=1}^{\ell} \left( \frac{k}{2\pi i(1+\varepsilon)} -1\right) k > \frac{k^2}{2\pi + 1} \left(\sum_{i=1}^{\ell} \frac{1}{i}\right) - \left(\sum_{i=1}^{\ell} k\right) > \frac{k^2 \ln(l+1)}{2\pi + 1} - n'. \end{align*} Recall that, by choice of $k$, we have $k \geq \sqrt{\frac{{6m}}{{1+\ln (n/k)}}}$ and in particular $k \geq \sqrt{\frac{6m}{1+\ln \ell}}$. Combining this fact with $\ln(\ell+1) \geq (1+\ln \ell)/2$ and $2m/9 \geq n'$ gives us the lower bound as follows: $$ m' \geq \left(\frac{6m}{1+\ln \ell }\right) \left(\frac{\ln(\ell+1)}{2\pi + 1}\right) - n' \geq \frac{3m}{2\pi + 1} - \frac{2m}{9} > \frac{3m}{9} - \frac{2m}{9}=\frac{m}{9}. $$ That is, for any values of $n$ and $m \in \{9n,\dots,\lfloor n^2/6 \rfloor\}$, we can construct a set of $n'$ unit disks with $m'$ intersecting pairs.
nodes.statement_short: Show $\lceil m/9\rceil\le m'\le 6m$.

nodes.name: Claim opener
nodes.statement: We now show that the number $m'$ of intersecting pairs in $\cal{D}$ satisfies $\lceil m/9 \rceil \leq m' \leq 6m$.
nodes.statement_short: State the bounds on $m'$ to be shown.

nodes.name: Arc length gamma_i
nodes.statement: Let $x_i$ denote the number of intersecting pairs of disks on the $i$-th layer, and let $\gamma_i$ be the arc length of $C_i$ such that two unit disks centered at two endpoints of the arc touch each other (see \figurename~\ref{fig:lowerBound}, middle). Note that two disks on the same layer overlap if and only if the arc distance between the centers is $\gamma_i$ or less, and disks in different layers cannot intersect.
nodes.statement_short: Define per-layer pair counts $x_i$ and the touching arc length $\gamma_i$.

nodes.name: Count pairs per layer
nodes.statement: Since the disks are evenly spaced on $C_i$, each disk of ${\cal D}_i$ intersects $2\lfloor \frac{\gamma_i}{4\pi i(1+\varepsilon)/k} \rfloor $ other disks. Taking into account that there are $k$ disks in ${\cal D}_i$ (and each crossing is counted twice), we obtain that $x_i= \lfloor\frac{\gamma_ik}{4\pi i(1+\varepsilon)}\rfloor k$ and thus the total number of intersecting pairs is $m'=\sum_{i=1}^{\ell} x_i = \sum_{i=1}^{\ell} \lfloor\frac{\gamma_ik}{4\pi i(1+\varepsilon)}\rfloor k$.
nodes.statement_short: $m'=\sum_i\lfloor\gamma_i k/(4\pi i(1+\varepsilon))\rfloor k$.

nodes.name: Bounds on gamma_i
nodes.statement: By using some trigonometric properties and picking a sufficiently small $\varepsilon$, we can show that, regardless of the value of $i$, we have $$2 < \gamma_i = 4i(1+\varepsilon)\sin^{-1}(1/2i(1+\varepsilon)) < 2\pi/3.$$
nodes.statement_short: $2<\gamma_i<2\pi/3$.

nodes.name: Upper bound on m'
nodes.statement: We now bound $m'$ from above. Since $\gamma_i< 2\pi/3$, we have $$m' < \sum_{i=1}^{\ell} \frac{ k^2}{6 i(1+\varepsilon)} < \frac{k^2}{6}\sum_{i=1}^{\ell} \frac{1}{i} < k^2(1+\ln \ell)/6 < k^2(1+\ln (2n/k))/6.$$ Recall that we choose $k$ to be the smallest natural number $k'$ such that $k' \geq \sqrt{\frac{{6m}}{{1+\ln (n/k')}}}$. We combine this bound with the assumption that $n<m$ to obtain the desired bound: \begin{align*} m' &< k^2\frac{(1+\ln (2n/k))}{6} < \left(1+\sqrt{\frac{{6m}}{{1+\ln (n/k)}}}\right)^2 \left(\sqrt{\frac{(1+2\ln (n/k))}{6}}\right)^2 \\ &< \left(\sqrt{\frac{1+2\ln (n/k)}{6}}+\sqrt{2m} \right)^2 <\left(\sqrt{\frac{6n}{6}}+\sqrt{2m} \right)^2 \\ &< (\sqrt{m}+\sqrt{2m})^2 =(3+2\sqrt{2}) m. \end{align*}
nodes.statement_short: Harmonic sums and the choice of $k$ give $m'<(3+2\sqrt2)m$.

nodes.name: Lower bound on m'
nodes.statement: For the lower bound we now use that $\gamma_i>2$ (and $\varepsilon \leq \frac{1}{2\pi}$). Recall that \begin{align*} m' &= \sum_{i=1}^{\ell} \left\lfloor\frac{\gamma_ik}{4\pi i(1+\varepsilon)}\right\rfloor k > \sum_{i=1}^{\ell} \left( \frac{k}{2\pi i(1+\varepsilon)} -1\right) k > \frac{k^2}{2\pi + 1} \left(\sum_{i=1}^{\ell} \frac{1}{i}\right) - \left(\sum_{i=1}^{\ell} k\right) > \frac{k^2 \ln(l+1)}{2\pi + 1} - n'. \end{align*} Recall that, by choice of $k$, we have $k \geq \sqrt{\frac{{6m}}{{1+\ln (n/k)}}}$ and in particular $k \geq \sqrt{\frac{6m}{1+\ln \ell}}$. Combining this fact with $\ln(\ell+1) \geq (1+\ln \ell)/2$ and $2m/9 \geq n'$ gives us the lower bound as follows: $$ m' \geq \left(\frac{6m}{1+\ln \ell }\right) \left(\frac{\ln(\ell+1)}{2\pi + 1}\right) - n' \geq \frac{3m}{2\pi + 1} - \frac{2m}{9} > \frac{3m}{9} - \frac{2m}{9}=\frac{m}{9}. $$
nodes.statement_short: Using $\gamma_i>2$ gives $m'>m/9$.

nodes.name: Conclusion on m'
nodes.statement: That is, for any values of $n$ and $m \in \{9n,\dots,\lfloor n^2/6 \rfloor\}$, we can construct a set of $n'$ unit disks with $m'$ intersecting pairs.
nodes.statement_short: The construction realizes the required $n',m'$.

nodes.name: Origin is a centerpoint
nodes.statement: By symmetry, we can see that the origin is a centerpoint of the centers of disks in $\cal{D}$.
nodes.statement_short: By symmetry the origin is a centerpoint.

nodes.name: Reduce to rays
nodes.statement: Thus, it remains to show that any line that passes through the origin must intersect many disks of ${\cal D}$. In the following we show something stronger: any ray emanating from a point $p$ inside $C_1$ will cross $\Omega( \sqrt{m\log (n/\sqrt{m})})$ disks.
nodes.statement_short: Show the stronger statement that every ray from inside $C_1$ meets many disks.

nodes.name: Coverage of each circle
nodes.statement: We count the number of intersections on each layer independently. Each unit disk in ${\cal D}_i$ covers $\frac{\gamma_i}{2i(1+\varepsilon)}$ radians of $C_i$. Since there are $k$ evenly spread disks in ${\cal D}_i$ and $\varepsilon \leq \frac{1}{4\pi}$, each point of the circle $C_i$ is contained in at least $\lfloor \frac{\gamma_i k}{2i(1+\varepsilon)} \cdot \frac{1}{2\pi} \rfloor > \frac{\gamma_i k}{i(4\pi +1)} - 1$ disks.
nodes.statement_short: Each point of $C_i$ lies in at least $\gamma_i k/(i(4\pi+1))-1$ disks.

nodes.name: Sum over layers
nodes.statement: By substituting $k \geq \sqrt{\frac{6m}{1+\ln \ell}}$, $\gamma_i > 2$, $\ln(\ell+1) \geq (1+\ln \ell)/2$, $\ell = n'/k$ and $2m/9 \geq n'$, we obtain that the number of disks in ${\cal D}$ intersected by the ray is at least \begin{align*} \sum_{i=1}^{\ell} (\frac{\gamma_i k}{i(4\pi +1)} - 1) & > \frac{2}{4\pi + 1}\left(\sqrt{\frac{6m}{1+\ln \ell }}\right)\left( \sum_{i=1}^{\ell} \frac{1}{i}\right) - \ell\\ & \geq \frac{2}{4\pi + 1} \left(\sqrt{\frac{6m}{1+\ln \ell}}\right)\ln(\ell +1) - \frac{n' \sqrt{1+\ln \ell}}{\sqrt{6m}}\\ & \geq \frac{\sqrt{6m (1+\ln \ell )}}{4\pi + 1} - \frac{2m}{9} \sqrt{\frac{1+\ln \ell}{6m}}\\ & \geq \left(\frac{\sqrt{6}}{4\pi + 1} - \frac{2}{9\sqrt{6}}\right) \sqrt{m(1+\ln \ell)} = \Omega( \sqrt{m\log (n/\sqrt{m})}). \tag*{\qed} \end{align*}
nodes.statement_short: Summing over layers gives $\Omega(\sqrt{m\log(n/\sqrt m)})$ crossings.

nodes.name: Nested construction
nodes.statement: Our construction is similar to the one of Theorem~\ref{thm:lowerjoint_unit}: let ${\cal C}_1$ be the set containing the unit disk centered at the origin. For $i>1$, let $D_i$ be the smallest enclosing disk containing all disks of ${\cal C}_{i-1}$. The set ${\cal C}_i$ (for $i>1$) is defined as the set containing the six disks of the same radius as $D_i$ surrounding $D_i$, such that each two consecutive disks touch and none overlap. Note that $D_i\not\in {\cal C}_{i}$ and ${\cal C}=\bigcup_{i=1}^n {\cal C}_i$.
nodes.statement_short: Recursively surround the enclosing disk by six equal disks.

nodes.name: Make disks disjoint
nodes.statement: Observe that in this construction disks of one level touch only neighbors on the same level (and on the next and previous level). We fix this by rotating the construction so that disks in ${\cal C}_i$ are tangent to $D_i$ but do not intersect with the disks of ${\cal C}_{i-1}$ (see Figure~\ref{fig:lowerBound} right). Tangencies can afterwards be removed by shirking the disks by a factor of $1-\varepsilon$ for a sufficiently small value of $\varepsilon$. We also shrink the disk in ${\cal C}_1$ by this factor of $1-\varepsilon$. After these two changes the disks will be pairwise disjoint.
nodes.statement_short: Rotate and shrink by $1-\varepsilon$ to make all disks pairwise disjoint.

nodes.name: Balanced line crosses many layers
nodes.statement: The argument is now similar to the one in Theorem~\ref{thm:lowerjoint_unit}, and the centers of the disks in $\cal C$ are placed in concentric circles around the origin. The main difference now is that each layer has a constant number of disks. Thus, any line $\ell$ that makes a balanced separator must cross $\Omega(n)$ concentric circles.
nodes.statement_short: With constantly many disks per layer, a balanced line crosses $\Omega(n)$ circles.

nodes.name: Conclude
nodes.statement: For every two intersections we can find at least one disk that intersects with $\ell$, and thus the $\Omega(n)$ lower bound follows. \qed
nodes.statement_short: Every two circle crossings yield an intersected disk, so $\Omega(n)$.

nodes.name: Find centerpoint
nodes.statement: find a centerpoint (which can be done in linear time~\cite{DBLP:journals/dcg/JadhavM94})
nodes.statement_short: Compute a centerpoint in linear time.

nodes.name: Try random lines
nodes.statement: try random lines passing through that point until a good separator is found.
nodes.statement_short: Sample random lines through the centerpoint until one is a good separator.

nodes.name: Random slope
nodes.statement: for a slope $a$ selected uniformly at random
nodes.statement_short: Draw a slope uniformly at random.

nodes.name: Best separator of that slope
nodes.statement: find a $2/3$-separator with slope $a$ that intersects the minimum number of disks (this step can be done in $O(n \log n)$ time by sorting the disks in orthogonal direction of $a$ and making a plane sweep)
nodes.statement_short: Sort disks orthogonally to $a$ and sweep to find the lightest $2/3$-separator of slope $a$.

nodes.name: Repeat
nodes.statement: We repeat this process many times to obtain a good line separator.
nodes.statement_short: Repeat many times and keep a good separator.

nodes.name: Build arrangement graph
nodes.statement: First, we build the arrangement of curves, and obtain a plane graph whose vertex set are the vertices of the arrangement and consecutive vertices on a curve are joined by an edge.\footnote{The method of Fox and Pach needs to add a constant number of additional vertices, but the main feature is that the overall complexity of the graph is $O(m+n)$.}
nodes.section: 4.1 The Method by Fox and Pach
nodes.statement_short: Build the arrangement as a plane graph.

nodes.name: Triangulate
nodes.statement: We triangulate the obtained plane graph to make it maximal planar.
nodes.section: 4.1 The Method by Fox and Pach
nodes.statement_short: Triangulate to a maximal planar graph.

nodes.name: Simple cycle separator
nodes.statement: Then, we find a simple cycle $2/3$-separator $C$ (i.e., a $2/3$-separator that forms a cycle in the graph) of size $O(\sqrt{m+n})$, which always exists \cite{DBLP:journals/jcss/Miller86}.
nodes.section: 4.1 The Method by Fox and Pach
nodes.statement_short: Find a simple cycle $2/3$-separator of size $O(\sqrt{m+n})$.

nodes.name: Output curves
nodes.statement: We output all curves containing a vertex in $C$.
nodes.section: 4.1 The Method by Fox and Pach
nodes.statement_short: Output the curves touching the cycle.
